{{Short description|Study of protein networks in biology}}
{{Distinguish|Toponymy}}
'''Toponomics''' is a discipline in [[systems biology]], [[Cell biology|molecular cell biology]], and [[histology]] concerning the study of the [[toponome]] of organisms.<ref name="ref1">{{cite book|last=Schubert|first=W|title=Topological Proteomics, Toponomics, MELK-Technology.|journal=Advances in Biochemical Engineering/Biotechnology|year=2003|isbn=978-3-540-00546-9|volume=83|pages=189–209|doi=10.1007/3-540-36459-5_8|pmid=12934931}}</ref><ref name="ref2">{{cite book|last=Schubert|first=W|title=Encyclopedia of Systems Biology|publisher=Springer New York|year=2013|isbn=978-1-4419-9862-0|pages=2191–2212|chapter=Toponomics|doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-9863-7_631}}</ref> It is the field of study that proposes to decode the complete toponome in health and disease (the human toponome project)<ref name="ref6">{{cite journal|last=Cottingham|first=Katie|date=May 2008|title=Human Toponome Project {{!}} Human Proteinpedia is open for (free) business|journal=Journal of Proteome Research|volume=7|issue=5|pages=1806|doi=10.1021/pr083701k|doi-access=}}</ref>—which is the next big challenge in human [[biotechnology]] after having decoded the human genome.<ref name="ref6" /><ref name="ref7">{{cite journal|last=Abott|first=A|date=12 October 2006|title="Mapping togetherness" (research highlight referring to Schubert et al. 2006)|journal=Nature|volume=443|issue=7112|pages=608–609|bibcode=2006Natur.443..608.|doi=10.1038/443608a|doi-access=free}}</ref>

A '''toponome''' is the [[spatial network]] code of proteins and other [[Biomolecule|biomolecules]] in [[Morphology (biology)|morphologically]] intact cells and tissues.<ref name="ref2" /><ref name="ref3">{{cite journal|last=Schubert|first=Walter|author2=Bonnekoh, Bernd |author3=Pommer, Ansgar J |author4=Philipsen, Lars |author5=Böckelmann, Raik |author6=Malykh, Yanina |author7=Gollnick, Harald |author8=Friedenberger, Manuela |author9=Bode, Marcus |author10= Dress, Andreas W M |title=Analyzing proteome topology and function by automated multidimensional fluorescence microscopy|journal=Nature Biotechnology|date=1 October 2006|volume=24|issue=10|pages=1270–1278|doi=10.1038/nbt1250 |pmid=17013374|s2cid=30436820}}</ref>

The spatial organization of biomolecules in cells is directly revealed by [[imaging cycler microscopy]] with parameter- and dimension-unlimited functional resolution. The resulting toponome structures are hierarchically organized and can be described by a three symbol code.<ref name="ref1" /><ref name="ref3" /><ref name="ref4">{{cite journal|last=Schubert|first=Walter|date=June 2007|title=A three-symbol code for organized proteomes based on cyclical imaging of protein locations|journal=Cytometry Part A|volume=71A|issue=6|pages=352–360|doi=10.1002/cyto.a.20281|pmid=17326231|s2cid=3132423|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="ref5">{{cite web|last=Schubert|first=W|title=Direct, spatial imaging of randomly large supermolecules by using parameter unlimited TIS imaging cycler microscopy.|url=http://www.toposnomos.com/doku/MC2013.pdf|accessdate=2013-09-23|publisher=International Microscopy Conference 2013}}</ref>

== Etymology ==
The terms ''toponome'' and ''toponomics'' were introduced in 2003 by Walter Schubert based on observations with [[Imaging Cycler Microscopy|imaging cycler microscopes (ICM)]].<ref name="ref1" />

''Toponome'' derived from the ancient Greek nouns ''topos'' (τόπος, 'place, position') and '''nomos''<nowiki/>' (νόμος, 'law'). Hence ''toponomics'' is a descriptive term addressing the fact that the spatial network of biomolecules in cells follows [[Topology|topological]] rules enabling coordinated actions.<ref name="ref1" />
